From like a center's perspective, what are like some of the little things that you have to really hone in on to make sure that like everything looks the same so you can build up a lot of different plays off of the same look? >> Uh you know, I think part of the the way you attack the line of scrimmage, you know, if you're running a naked uh there's certain ways to do it. I mean, with like a quarterback boot out and you can attack that the line of scrimmage like you're running an outside zone and stretch and and so, you're kind of you're treating it like you're running an outside zone and you're seeing how that D-lineman's going to react. So, when you do run outside zone, you know how it's going to react and and you're kind of playing those like mental games like all game figuring out, you know, attacking him this way and then running a naked and just figuring out how they're going to react and are they two gappers or are they jetters and how you need your hand placement and and so just making things look the same and you know, coming up to line of scrimmage making calls or points, making everything look and feel the same until it's not. And I think uh even just going under center, it just it helps you do so many things that look the same. >> Can you talk about the chemistry that Coach Kooper had back in the OTAs to what it is now with with the offensive line room? >> Yeah, I think uh I think it just keeps growing. Just understanding him and how he coaches and how he approaches things and how he likes to work and just going through and doing the individual drills, you know, maybe there's a day like today where, you know, we are feeling it, we're exhausted, you know, how does he change things up? How does he, you know, keep our legs light and just figuring him out? I mean, it's been nice and just uh figuring out, you know, how he ticks and how we tick and, you know, he's he's been doing a great job of figuring out how to coach certain guys and and adjust and make sure everybody's uh learning properly, you know, certain guys learn different ways. >> Sean said that the >> Go ahead. >> Let's go back to the schedule in the regular year and getting canceled. We were just uh like how do you look at the last couple years that you both learned about that process together? And it is a pretty new offense. I mean, what do you think those things have done to push that here? >> Uh well, I think it'll be good during the season because a lot of times, you know, we'll be running a lot of plays where one play would get checked to something different. You know, different each day. Where in the season, you know, we may come in and hey, this play's only getting checked to this. This play's only getting checked to this. And what are the parameters of the check? And you know, we can meet and look at the defense and see exactly how it looks. So, we're we're helping each other out with those checks. Where, you know, it'll be exciting when we get to that point during the season when things are set and solid where, you know, right now we're just we're running so many different things and trying to get a hang of it and get the flow. So, it'll be a little different during the season. >> I thought this summer it seems more confident, more self-assured to to me at least. Have you Have you gotten that from him? >> Yeah, I mean if you line up against Jalen Carter have pass rushes every day and you're doing as well as he is, I mean, he he is going to be confident. I mean, this this D-line's really good. and so, he's been doing a great job throughout camp and just consistent steady. He should be confident. He's He's playing some really good football. >> And to what extent have the pre-snap protections sometimes fallen on the offensive line, sometimes on the quarterback? I guess what's been the biggest difference relative to other schemes and how's how's everything going? >> Uh there's always a little carryover and crossover, but it's just making sure I mean you get the play call, you go up there and you're being consistent with your calls and making sure everybody hears you and understands you and it's it's similar, but it's not the same. And everybody has different responsibilities and you know, somebody may be responsible to give an alert to someone or see a certain thing and you got to have eyes in you certain spots. It and we just have a little bit more protections where we may go in and out of like maybe a man protection or a slide protection or a gap protection. It's just I feel like we might have a little bit more in our arsenal now. >> How how has Shawn as a play caller, coordinator, teacher, developer, whatever you want to say from the start of OTAs until now. Like, what do you think's the biggest difference that you've seen getting more comfortable? >> Uh being consistent in, you know, what he harps on and what he's frustrated at. You know, he You're always going to be frustrated when somebody gives an MAA, a a missed assignment, you know, they they do the wrong job and it's like a mental error and that's something that is frustrating and needs to be coached and you know, he does a good job at harping at that. And then like other things that, you know, maybe confusion from a call or a certain communication. He does a great job at talking through it and why it's that way and why it should be called a certain way and he's just he's consistent in what he um coaches hard on and what he you know, wants to talk through and coach and he does a good job at it. >> Cool. All right, thanks again. >> Thanks, guys. Appreciate >> If it was saying earlier, sometimes things just click for guys. >> What clicked for you and did you feel like you're getting close to having like a breakthrough of some sort? >> I mean, just the you know, the work I put in all that in the off season, you know, I you know, I'm I come from a place where you know, I was playing a lot in in college and you know, that's just kind of the the player I am. Like I want to go out there and contribute and and do my part for the team and and the organization. So, you know, just uh being able to be around the guys and coach Hurt and and Q, like to help build that confidence going into this camp, like you know, I just you know, wanted to make my presence known uh and you know, I'm still working to do that. >> What are the mental challenges when you aren't getting on the field maybe as much as you would like to last year and and trying to I guess I don't know, reframe the way that you approach the the day? >> feel like, you know, you just well, I feel like you just got to do better, right? Like uh you know, last year wasn't good enough. So, you know, I can't do the same thing I did uh prior to that. Obviously, I needed to change some things up. So, you know, I get when I did it my training in the off season, I really focused on those uh those key aspects I felt like I needed to improve. Uh and then, you know, just coming out here and and you know, trusting myself and and you know, being confident that what I did in the off season off season does work and you know, help propel me to to get in that role. >> What did you want to focus on in the off season and how have you seen that kind of pay off now? >> Yeah, so you know, me and coach Hurt, you know, as we had our exit meetings, you know, a lot of it was, you know, block destruction and and mobility and flexibility. You know, I always knew the strength was there, but now it was, you know, how do I use it in a functional movement, you know, and and out there on the field without being too stiff or being too lopsided. So, you know, I really I stayed here for the off season and and worked with our our strength staff who who've been amazing. You know, I've probably talked their ears off more than enough to kind of figure out, you know, what what needs to be done, but you know, I'm just going to continue to to keep doing that. >> Has that flexibility and and mobility led to maybe quicker releases off of the ball at the at the start of the play? >> Oh, yeah, 100% you know, being able to, you know, kind of sit more in my stance, you know, kind of feel more power through my legs and core being down in my stance. Uh And then obviously, you know, with you know, a year under my belt being able to have the the experience of going against an NFL offense and kind of how, you know, those work. Now, you know, I feel a lot more confident when I'm out there, you know, looking at the formations, looking at the personnel and kind of, you know, understanding what what possibilities I can get. >> What have been some of your biggest impact moments in the last few >> I mean, you know, you love to make those plays, but you know, I can't do it without the guys in in the room and on the line. So, you know, without them, you know, it doesn't really mean much, you know, this week, you know, as you know, I'm still trying to get mine, you know, go get mine. You know, I'm rooting for the the fellows next to me too to go get theirs. >> How have those guys helped you like specifically JC Jackson, Jordan Davis, like how have they helped you at all like >> Yeah, that's yeah, no. JC and JD and Moro and you know, even BY like, you know, we're always talking football especially in the meetings like, you know, even today I was just asking him about JC about, you know, a certain type of block and how he's just able to basically destroy that block and and be disruptive getting off, you know, shedding the block to make the tackle. You know, just kind of getting little technique things from them and just kind of, you know, pieces of advice that they've seen throughout the years. >> How did you guys I mean, JC obviously is kind of gifted in that particular area. Is that kind of hard like he's so old and stuff? >> Yeah, you know, obviously I'm not going to say like I'm going to go out there and replicate what he's doing, you know, but at the same time it's like, okay, this is what he's thinking of when when he sees this type of stuff, maybe I can think of it in that same regard and do it my way or do it a way that I know that I can be successful, too. So, it's not necessarily doing, you know, copying him or or copying any of the guys, but it's more so taking that information that they give me and and applying it to myself. >> Did you get discouraged at all last year and how did you kind of deal with that when if if it happened? >> I mean, I don't know if I'm going to say discouraged, you know, I definitely was was disappointed, uh you know, in myself just cuz, you know, I just it just wasn't to my standard and you know, I took it personal in the off-season and after the after the season, you know, when they they told me they still, you know, see a lot of hope in me and have a lot of a lot of a lot of uh you know, gifts and you know, they they still have a lot of faith in me like it it kind of uh made me think that I needed to, you know, step it up, you know, they believe in me, so why can't I believe in myself? >> What's it like working with you and getting to know him a little bit? And you are getting to know >> Man, U R is he is one special guy. Like he is he's so soft-spoken and so quiet, but he's also one of the funniest guys on the team and you know, like he he loves to to bring that juice, especially I got practice and you know, I think just trying to help him, you know, work he's trying to cram what what would you say that up? 15 years of football experience in the span of 4 months like he's taking a lot in right now and he's taking the coaching very well and you know I could definitely we definitely see him getting frustrated with himself you know as as normal football players do because you know he's not able to get it on the first try and then we just had to keep reminding him like dude you just started playing football like it's going to take some time for you to understand what's what's needed and asked of you and like what you can do like he is a physical specimen like he's once he gets it figured out like nothing can stop him. >> You mentioned that last night that he got a chance to break down the the group a couple of times you already you remember what those moments were like and then how he did it? >> I mean yeah you know it's just like like you know normal football chance like but that's just like what he knows about you know the sport of football and so when he gets in the middle and he starts doing one of those chance like it gets the guys you know pretty fired up cuz he kind of brings the juice and then next thing you know he's jumping you know 7 ft in the air above everybody and it's like you kind of again you can see that like holy like this dude is a freak and so just knowing that if we can get that you know kind of energy and confidence especially when he's out there on the field like I said he's going to be unstoppable. >> And what kind of energy does he show that juice and energy during the week at practice in the building in general? >> I mean yeah you know we're just you know just a bunch of guys we just you know we hang out with each other all day basically especially during camp and just getting to talk to him and you know learn about his life back home and and his family and you know what he's had to go through to get here and you know you you start to build that real true connection that true relationship you know it it it means more like you know like we we truly want like feel for him and want him to be successful while he's here. >> How high can you jump? >> Me? >> Uh not as high as him but I definitely can get up there though for a big fella. >> All right good. >> Mhm. >> How we doing? Well. >> Saw Mekhi Leven get back out there and what's it been like building chemistry with him on the field? >> Just continue to stack. He's hungry, eager, excited. I feel like he's learned a lot just in this short time being in the league and really he's been very direct and forward about trying to take care of his body and all the things that he can be better in and that so I'm happy to have him back out there on the grass. He's a great player. >> How do you think you performed in this camp from your personal perspective? >> I feel like it was a good camp. Taking in the coaching, taking in the the time and the growth that comes with a camp. Um feel like Sean has been great. Great to ask questions and um really great great camp to learn from so >> Geno, what do you learn from interceptions in practice? >> Say that again. >> you learn from interceptions? >> I think generally speaking you learn from every play um like regardless how the result is especially when you're putting in something new I think every time we come out here and we get a chance to get on the grass you want to take the coaching and apply be aggressive in it and then with your experiences you reflect on them think about them and you say okay you can play the game in this type of way you can play the game in that type of way and so um I think I used the term calibrating with you guys that you know all of that that whole entire process builds kind of your mind on how you're calculated you know when when you play the game and so um it's been a really good camp I'm happy about the experiences that we've had to be able to grow from them was very excited about the opportunity to be able to practice with um you know the guys our our receiving core when you know the the guys that are going to start are we're we're banged up and so just to have the time to build chemistry build experiences with everyone as a unit I feel like that was very valuable >> How much of the offense do you guys do you think the team has down to this point how's the installation process been going two and a half weeks ahead of the first game >> Yeah you know it's it's going it's it's been you know a lot of new information a lot of new things and nothing very specific on kind of uh one direction of what we can be um it's a multi-faceted offense and approach and you know when you get to game planning I'm sure they even get more fine and fine and very direct to what we want to do that week >> With how multi-faceted it is where do you think your command of the overall offense >> Yeah I feel like I'm in a good spot feel like I'm in a good spot think it's all about really looking at the experiences the experiences don't mean anything until you reflect on them and you grow from them and you start to apply them and so um we're very widespread in what we're doing right now and I think that's good so when we can hone it down and kind of see who we are you know, establish what exactly that identity is for us and we you know, it's it'll it'll kind of come together. So, still very early. >> You used the term multifaceted. I guess with you know, the changes that Shawn brings versus what you guys have done previously that you were successful in. I guess the big question is how much will we keep and how much you won't keep. But in this offense with Shawn and so much predicated on the center and that kind of stuff, does it allow a lot for that to happen? Um in terms of keeping what the previous offense >> Yeah, I think that's a a great question and it's something that you keep in mind of when you've had so much success. So, you know, well, how will it look? You don't really know. Do you want to win? Absolutely. So, we got to figure out who we are as a team. Um obviously coaches come in with a great mindset, great philosophy and putting everything together. Brings us a bit more structure. Um in the end, it's um it's about what going to what's going to go out there and be the best for our team. And so, um I know Shawn will come up with the answer to that over time. >> How do you think you've been around him now for five or six months? Where do you think he's grown the most? How's that process going? >> Yeah, want to honor that question cuz it's still really early. Uh still really early. So, when we get into the season, you know, we'll begin to find out a lot about ourselves. Um to this point, it's just been a lot of teaching. Um a lot of teaching, a lot of opportunities to get on the grass and teaching off of that. And so, once we put plans together, build identity going one direction, um you know, you can see it a little clearly then. >> Do you agree what kind of correlation have you found between camp performance and in-season performance both for you and for the team? >> Um I haven't I haven't thought about it much. Um I think as time has gone on, I've just look at each year as its own. Um I've got a a diligence that I have about just approaching change and new new coaching new perspective, new voice. And I think that's where it all starts. Um Performance is definitely important, but the relationship that you have and the conversations that you can have in the process is is really where it all starts. And so I've been in sponge mode this whole entire time taking in the perspective that coach has, um his eye for the game. And just going out there and trying to apply that. And so when you get into the game what's the goal? You know, the goal is to win. So that that always trumps. >> With this being the to the last several weeks, late July to this point now, what's been the biggest improvement for the offense in your >> With this being the final day of camp, you think back to the last several weeks, late July now we're in August, what's been the biggest improvement throughout that time in your eyes? >> Uh I think just been able to build chemistry as a team. Feel like we've been able to come together, been able to compete, have some fun moments together. So that's what I value from this camp. >> We haven't seen you all that much through July stocks. We haven't seen much of you in camp. >> Yeah, he had he had No, he's been healthy. Hasn't been healthy what these last >> Yeah, just the last few I just meant like >> Previously working mostly with the twos and threes. I'm just wondering, knowing how important chemistry is with you and Yeah. No, he hadn't been up with that unit um a lot this camp, but he's he's got a lot of talent. You know, he got a lot of talent. We spent some time in the summertime, so not not foreign from it. but I think you know, once you kind of know where you are, know your role, I think that's something that can be a quick fix. >> Do you see the offense as something that's going to continue to evolve into the season? And I'm not assuming that's probably no different than past years, but is there a kind of a difference like with you know, how this offense evolves going forward compared to the others? I mean, I just think about the foundation of what you are, foundation of what is introduced to be. And so, from a you know, intent and the North Star uh structure standpoint, the foundation of it. I think it's I think it's been clear and we've been driving that and um as you see who you have on your team and you begin to progress forward, you hone things down and you say, "This is who we are. This is you know, how I want to lead it." So, I I think that's where Sean is. Um and you know, a lot of that is is up for him to mold and put together, so with the in the end, we can go out there and be in the best position to win. >> Hey, there's obviously a a backup quarterback competition. As a As a starter, what do you want in a backup? What's important to you as a starter? >> Well, I think all three guys have been very valuable to the room. Um they've got a lot of wisdom, a lot of talent. Um and I value the perspective. So, >> I saw you guys >> Kai a little bit. Um the wide receiver group as a whole, now that you've gotten this done, gotten extra reps with some of the new guys, what do you What do you think of the group as a whole? >> Yeah, I'm I'm excited excited for the group. Um you know, I think just the time that we've been able to put together, uh put in together over the summer, um the reps that we've had, the conversations that we've been able to have about how we can grow Um and I think anytime you're playing with a new unit it's just about being on the same page and that's no different than that's no different than than coaching too. When you've got a new play caller, you've got new voice, you've got new perspective everybody's chasing the same thing. Everybody wants the same outcome. Everybody process looks a little different so being able to get that being able to navigate how does our process look? How does this look for this unit? This team sounds like a broken record a bit from you know, what I've said in the past but you know, what is this team? What is the this iteration of the Eagles going to look like? So I think the think think this camp is giving us an opportunity to come closer to that and we've still got a time before we we tee it off and it's you know, live ball but we we just want to continue to progress every day keep the uh communication open, being on the same page, being aligned and going out there and doing it together as a team. >> Okay, thanks y'all. Thanks everybody for coming in for today.

title: Football at Four: More on Eagles New Offense and Fangio Comments
text: And Football at Four is powered by the Inside the Birds podcast. It's brought to you by the FanDuel Sportsbook at Ocean Casino Resort in Atlantic City. Football at Four, Jeff Mosher from the Inside the Birds podcast and PhillyVoice.com as the Eagles had their open practice last night, which is almost kind of like a preseason game, if you will. You almost get more out of that than you do the preseason games because the starters are on the field. What did we learn? We heard from Vic Fangio earlier today. We heard from Nick Sirianni before the practice yesterday. Somebody actually brought up an interesting point, Jeff Mosher. At what point are is the NFL going to scrap the preseason games and just have the joint practices available to the public and use those as the games that you could pay to go see. Now, that's the next evolution of preseason games, is it not? >> Well, it might be. I mean, they're they're probably going to go to two preseason games once they go to an 18 um regular season game. So, uh they'll figure out a way to cut the lop off another preseason game and they'll continue to do That will actually make joint practices that much more important cuz now you only have two preseason games and everybody seems to love the work that you're able to get in in a joint practice. And I don't know if there's a bigger advocate for joint practices than Vic Fangio. I mean, he could give It feels like he wants to do press conferences just devoted to the value of joint practices and he felt that the Eagles got a lot of great work in uh against the Patriots. I think you mentioned something so 80 80 some odd reps in the on the first day of practice, which is a lot more than you get in a normal uh practice at your at your own facility. So, there's a lot of merit to them. >> Well, and I did hear him say that about how much they got out of it. Uh but the next iteration would be that you get to play in front of fans, so you can get some noise and you can get some atmosphere, but you can say, "Hey, we're going to run the next 15 plays from inside the red zone here, so we need a little noise in here." Something you can't do during the joint practices, so uh we'll see if the NFL does anything here because he did say that I thought one of the takeaways from what he said was also that uh he can't take a lot from certain people because you got to do it against front-line players. But how do you do it against front-line players when you're not playing against front-line players? >> Well, the way you're the way you're phrasing it though, it almost makes me think you you envision like the stadiums being filled with lots of fans and them trying to do that in in the big bigger stadiums as opposed to the the smaller practice facilities. Is that what you were getting at or >> Right, you could almost have an open practice like you did last night, but have an open joint practice. >> Uh yeah, but the problem with that, Mike, why I don't think that that's feasible to do much of is because you need for real joint practices to be valuable and those those 80 reps, you got to have multiple practice fields so that your first offense can go on against the other first defense and vice versa. Uh you need at least two good fields. So if you if you try to do these open practice open joint practices on a one-field stadium like the link or anything else, then you're limiting the amount of work you'd be able to get in. >> I got you. Um well, I mean, maybe you uh you remember >> second day. Maybe you do it one day at your facility >> Yes. Yeah, yeah, yeah. The second day is at that. Yeah, yeah. Well, like the old days at Lehigh, you would sit in the bleachers all day, right? You know, you can uh they don't do that anymore because of you know, they do it over at uh the Novacare or whatever. It's Thomas Jefferson now. Uh but that being said, let's take a look at some of the things from last night's game. Uh he got asked about Rick Woolen today multiple times. Uh two interceptions, one was a pick-six, and um where do you think that Woolen is in terms of the impact he'll have for this defense. >> Yeah, I think you know, Vic has been very clear with Woolen on two things. One, he likes him. He really likes what he brings. He likes him as a person, as a player. You know, he said that right from the start that he was going to be different than Seattle, which is interesting cuz they won the Super Bowl. He's going to use Woolen as a three-down, four-down corner. He is a starting corner. Whereas the Seahawks brought him off the field against the run. So, that's that's interesting right off the bat. Now, you've heard Vic also say that he just needs to be more consistent and clean up some technique issues that fail him at times. And we have seen that. We've seen the best and the worst of Woolen. You know, once training camp started, we've seen some really good games and last night he was good. And we've also seen him get beat on shiftier receivers because as a tall defensive back, he struggles with throttling down. Stiffer hips, that's just natural for a guy who has his length. But it's not just about that. I mean, Vic was pretty clear today that he's got some technique issues that he's got to clean up if he really wants to truly be a great cornerback. >> Which Vic acknowledged that Which Vic acknowledged that Woolen knows that he that he is sloppy at times. >> Yeah. And see to me, that goes beyond a little bit of the the stiffness that we're talking about. That's natural. That might not be ever something that Woolen can overcome because of how he's built. But technique, that's always coachable. That's always something you can correct and work on. And it almost sounded like Vic was saying that he just he lapses sometimes with his technique and he's got to be more consistent there. And if he could, then he'll be a Or, mean, a great the sky's the limit. If not, you're still getting a pretty good quarterback. >> Yeah. Uh football for Jeff Mosher >> be Vic. >> Josh Hunt very disruptive last night. Interesting question to Vic today. You know, hey, where is he in the third year? He's like, about where I wanted him to be. And what do you expect from him? I don't know. Uh what should we expect from Josh Hunt? Do you look at him now as their top edge rusher? >> Yeah, I mean, he it almost sounded like he was speaking negatively, but he was actually doing the opposite. He basically said, uh you know, I'll he'll have reached where he's reached when when all the reporters stop asking me if I'm surprised by how good he is. And Vic was basically saying, I'm not surprised anymore. I see it. He's he's done what we've asked him to do. He's going to be a starting edge. He has a chance to be a guy who probably has Pro Bowl level uh capabilities because he's so damn athletic. Um and he's really understanding the finer parts of Vic's defense now. So, that's why Vic Vic is basically saying, I'm running out of things to say about a guy who's now just been very consistent. And now he's like the other guys on the team that you don't ask about because you already Like Lane Johnson, nobody ever asks uh uh Mr. Howie, hey, are you surprised by how well Lane Johnson is doing? Right? Now, I'm not trying to put Josh Hunt in Lane Johnson's category, but what I'm just saying is nothing that Josh does anymore is a novel or taking the coach by surprise. >> Uh Jeff, Jalen Hurts the wheel route touchdown to Barkley, then a couple interceptions. Uh I don't know, up and down. What do you make of Hurts in this offense right now? And and what should What What is the the the expectations going into the first quarter of the season? >> Yeah, you know, I just watched their last practice in training camp. Um and it was kind of like what I've seen all throughout camp, just just a lot of short stuff. Nothing really nothing like past training camps where there would be a couple of bombs, you know, that was Jalen's always best throw. Um little choppy. And I said to Andrew, you know, if this if the Eagles weren't learning a new offense, if this was just a continuation of the last few years, man, would the me we would probably be really hard on the offense as a whole, I think Jalen Hurts, because it just it really hasn't looked pretty. And whenever you're in your sixth of a quarterback, you want to see like that point where training camp is a breeze because you don't get touched. Um and you you haven't seen that, but they are learning a new offense, and I'm not I'm not overly concerned about it. I do think that they're, you know, the whole I think the short stuff's important because this offense is going to be predicated on pitch and catch and some layup routes. Um I'm not totally Let me say I I I don't want to I don't want to be like too down, but I also want to be too praiseworthy cuz it really hasn't been >> No. >> poetry in motion. It really It really hasn't been what you would hope to see. Um but I just think I I think I've been telling you this for a while. I I think September's going to be a little bit of a struggle. Um and also they're going up against the defense, so a really good defense every day. >> Well, and then you've got the other like you're watching the team play, and I see Carson uh Steel with six catches. I'm thinking they're not going to throw the ball to the running back six times, or this is a completely new defense. Maybe they will. Uh last night he throws a touchdown to to uh Jalen Hurts. Am I supposed to think now that the running back will be a bigger factor in the pass game? >> I think the opportunity for the running back to be a big factor in the pass game has always been there in any offense, but it just hasn't been a part of the offense. And I I definitely will say I've seen more route diversity from the running backs this year. You know, I saw Saquon run a Texas route the other day in practice and I'm like, "Darn, I haven't seen a running back run a Texas route in quite a while in this offense." So, that's that's good. You mentioned the Saquon touchdown last night. It looked like a wheel that sort of evolved into a corner route, which makes me think that maybe there was either a sight adjustment or some leniency on Saquon's part about how he was allowed to run that route, which would also be a little bit of a new wrinkle in the offense. And Kyle Shanahan provided an update. >> He's doing good. Um hoping that he can get into practice next week and um we'll see how those three days go after their mandatory three days off. So, the 49ers take off to Las Vegas today. They play the Raiders tomorrow. Obviously, no Nick Bosa for any part of that. But then there are the three mandatory days off before practice next Monday and next Wednesday in Santa Clara before takeoff to Australia. So, you want to make sure that Nick Bosa gets reinvolved and that Nick Bosa is feeling good before you take off to Melbourne. Now, the ramp up plan for Nick Bosa has been relatively straightforward, but of course, there still is worry because he's coming off of his third ACL tear, including the second on the knee that he's been rehabbing over the course of this off season. That's why the tendonitis popped up in the first place, and that's why the 49ers moved to this unique week one ramp up plan for Bosa. And the next step involves that return to practice. They will continue scouring the edge rusher market. John Joiner who originally joined the league with the Raiders, still a younger defensive end, 6'4, about 260 plus pounds, worked out or visited the 49ers today, technically didn't work out. So maybe they do add Joiner ahead of the game on Thursday just to finish this preseason. And then of course you've got guys like Keon White who are back in the rotation for San Francisco and Mike Williams who's expected to start the season on pup but is going to be back at some point for the 49ers. This though is a BOSA dependent defense. We saw that last year. Big drop off after week three. And well we might see that this year. They're going to need Nick to be in there. I talked about all of this and more on 95.7 the game. Enjoy the full interview. uh our friend David Lombardi all over the 49er beat and a parent who doesn't have to deal with this yet uh because his child is not old enough for these kinds of worries. But David, you better get ready. It's coming. >> I'll I'll brace myself, but I'm a firm believer of cross that bridge when you get to it. So, I'm I'm on my bridge right now. Not on that one yet. >> Well, uh that's kind of like the uh the 49ers, isn't it? I mean, isn't that essentially what Kyle Shanahan says about these injuries? Like, a lot of guys were missing practice today. At the same time, uh, very few of them are currently slated as not available for two Thursdays from now. So, do you believe that the 49ers are quote unquote very injured or do you believe the opposite that they're actually kind of relatively healthy right now? Yeah, I think it's probably somewhere in the middle, but that's football. That's the nature of the sport. I think that 49ers fans and the media surrounding the 49ers has this PTSD from last year when yes, they were very injured, especially amongst the star players and we talked about it a bit on the practice field today. It was good to see you out there. the >> you too >> 49ers this year it started in a way that >> fueled the injury worry tsunami right because Ricky Pearl had the PCL flare up and and he had to have surgery that was the news right out of bed plus the 49ers were playing things extra cautiously Christian McCaffrey for example was out two weeks on purpose they're they're managing him So because it wasn't known exactly why they were doing what they were doing with McAffrey and you combine it with Pearl and all from last year, I think it turned into this whole thing on social media. This the substation looming in the background of every single practice video certainly fueled that as well. But I think right >> everybody around the league is dealing with injuries. I don't think the 49ers are dealing with an inordinate amount and I think they're being very very cautious because most of the guys on the long list of players who weren't available at practice today are expected back next week >> among them uh expected back next week. What is your read on Bosa and KD as far as their ability to make it back next week? >> Bosa is a really really unique circumstance because he's torn his ACL three times. This one was the second on the same knee. So, the tendonitis flared up. They are ramping him up in hopes for week one. And he goes into a different bucket than everyone else just because it is such an exceptional circumstance and because he is Nick Bosa. Kyle Shanahan today said that he hopes he's back on the practice field next week, which would be, you know, essentially two weeks ahead of the season opener against the Rams, and then he'll get on the flight to Australia. And the 49ers hope that the season will go well. It's obviously a worry. Like, you can't just say with a straight face that a guy who's torn his ACL three times does not give you worry of of another knee injury or another complication. It's obviously a worry, but the fact that he hadn't been at practice over the course of the last two weeks is not the root cause of that worry, right? And they're hoping to to bring him back here over the course of the the next two weeks of practice so he's ready for week one. On the front of KD, I mean, that that's turning into borderline miraculous recovery. He he he might only miss one game if he if he's back week one. He'll have only missed one game against the Seattle Seahawks in the playoffs. So that's it, Killies. And uh he's he's back out on the practice field now. >> David Lombardi with us here and dibs 957 the game. Can we get into the roster weeds with you? I'd love to do this. Let's start with left guard. How do you handicap that race right now? >> Well, Carver Willis has been taking the the starter reps for the 49ers. That's the rookie out of Washington. I think back though to what Chris Fer initially said about this race in spring. He said, "I'm not sure if one person's going to win this job." I think the 49ers were already ready for a platoon, which they ran last year at left guard way back in spring. The early leader on the outside seemed to be Connor Kby, but he definitely hasn't been the leader as of late. Robert Jones took over those first team duties for the 49ers, but he got hurt. However, he's one of the players whom they're expecting back next week. And I think that an outside surprise here, but one that we need to consider is Austin Pleasants, who's also supposed to be back at practice next week. He started in place with Trent Williams at left tackle, but you saw Pleasants playing some guard in the last preseason game, and he was also there in practice before that game against the Chargers. That's four options for the 49ers. I'm not saying they're going to run a four-man platoon, but I wouldn't be shocked if if you saw multiple guys rotate through during the regular season. Now, obviously, you want to narrow this down and ultimately you want to settle on somebody. But I will say, and I said this last year when they ran a platoon, if you if you don't have a clear winner, it's not the worst thing in the world to to run multiple guys out there because defensive linemen rotate and they stay fresh because of it. So, you can actually maintain a level of freshness from your offensive linemen if if you have two guys who you think are about equal. I'm not saying that this isn't a position of worry for the 49ers. It absolutely is. But I wouldn't act like a platoon if that's what they end up going to is something that's completely, you know, unprecedented. And Bill Walsh even platooned offensive linemen back in the day. So maybe we're heading in that direction. Are any of those guys you mentioned of the fourman rotation, are any of them at risk in not making the roster at all? >> Uh, yeah. I I think that somebody like Connor Colby here here's the thing. The roster 53 spots on it and they're going to have to be creative to keep all the guys they want to in the building. So, they're going to run a lot of injury maneuvers and and we're going to be talking about the pup list and we're going to be talking about IR return designations and all this and all that. Bottom line is that you can't carry everybody that you want to carry every year. And if you do not assert yourself as a starter at a particular position on the offensive line, so Connor Colby is an example here. I don't think he's asserted himself as the de facto starter yet at at left guard. What what teams will do is they'll audition you at other positions that you can play such as right guard to see if you have any backup utility because if you're not one of the starters, you almost have to be able to play multiple positions because you can't just be a backup at one spot. There just isn't enough roster room for that. So, for example, that's why I brought Colobby into the mix. If if they don't feel that he's one of their two best left guards, then he probably doesn't make the roster. Maybe he follows the Colton Mckitz path and he resigns the practice squad and that would be a great path to follow because Colton Mckivitz turned into a productive starter. But I think there's a I think there's a solid chance that that you know somebody like that doesn't make this 53 man but does stay in the building. David, there's a couple of undrafted guys I want to ask you about who I know have popped a little bit in camp, and I want to see if you think they're either going to make the team or get protected on the practice squad. Let's start with the defensive line and James Thompson Jr., what do you think they're going to do with him? >> I think he's making the team. I think that uh he is well more advanced than anybody really anticipated coming out of Illinois undrafted free agent 66 but he was making plays against the run against the Chargers and you know that's always the worry especially Alfred Collins it seems that he's still getting his legs back underneath him. He had a rough first game against the Titans where he was getting washed out of some of those run plays. And yeah, he's 6'7, right? He's tall. You always worry about these tall guys and the pad level and I think that James Thompson has really really acclimated to the NFL quickly and he also has pass rushing juice. So, I would expect James Thompson to make this 53man roster. >> And then what do they do with Larry Worth III? Let let everybody know what you know about him and and what you think the plan is. Well, all the hype is on Jaden Duggar, but Larry Worth is a similar player. He was a safety at Arkansas. He's really tall like Duggar. He's 6'4. Doesn't have the same wingspan, but Duggar has like a world record wingspan for linebackers. His wingspan longer than Alden Smith's to give you some perspective. So, Duggar's a little bit shorter than that, but still really, really long player, safety background. Today, we saw a nice pass breakup working against Jake Tongis. I mean, he's been he's been good in coverage for the 49ers. So, I think that he and Duggar kind of go together as as the prototypes for the feverback position that Raheem Morris is trying to implement. That super versatile position that can rush the passer, that can cover, that can play stack linebacker. I think in all likelihood, if you look at roster numbers, somebody like Duggar makes the 53 and worth the 49ers really want to keep around and and probably will be able to on the practice squad. and uh you know you start building up that arsenal of of extremely versatile long talent on the second level of the defense. >> You mentioned Worth as a possible sneak through candidate. Is there anyone else that you can see that the Niners maybe will try to hide on Thursday night in the hopes of having them clear waiverss and keep them on the squad? >> Well, I would have to pop open my roster and just just look. I'm thinking through different positions and and you talk about some of the rookies. I think, you know, most of these drafties probably going to make the team for San Francisco. The the thing about this is that they have a lot of guys right now, as we discussed, with with relatively minor injuries. So, it's really really hard to predict and project exactly what the initial 53 is going to look like. Again, I have to emphasize it's just the initial 53. That thing is going to change so many times over the course of this season, but they're going to be running a lot of injury maneuvers. Just be ready for this, okay? Just be ready. Here's one thing. Like, as far as sneaking guys through, I think Isaac Gendo right now, they thought he was they're going to be ready near the start of training camp. For all I know, he's ready to go coming off the torn pectoral muscle. But keeping him on top right now has big advantages for the 49ers because if he stays there, then he doesn't take up a 53man roster spot and can start practicing due to the new rules by week three. He can't return until week five. But still, you could see how keeping Gendo and Mike Williams on pump and especially Greno, even though he might be healthy right now, allows the 49ers to buy more roster spots and therefore protect more players from waiverss. >> You're listening to 957 the game KGMZ FM and HC1 San Francisco and Odyssey Sports Station in the home of the Golden State Warriors and Valkyries. Plus, you know, in his case, his stature, I think, helps him for that particular job for punt returner because, you know, he's shorter. He's 5'9 and there's real short area quickness there. So, he did it a lot in college and I think he entered this camp as the favorite to be the 49ers punt returner just because of his explosiveness and uh because of his experience at that position. Now, then came the complicating factors. I mean, and and the first of which was rooted in last year. He went to hell and back. He tore his hamstring four times last year, so he's unable to play. So, the 49ers had to see him uh get healthy and and stay healthy. And that actually has been a challenge here over this training camp. So, some doubt really, I think, started to creep in with everybody, but with the coaching staff, especially. So when he returned that punt 83 yards for a touchdown, I think what it did was quiet a lot of the doubt and it reminded the 49ers that they needed a reminder of why you believed in this guy because you saw that explosiveness and the punt return ability right on display over there at Sofi Stadium. So um it was a big moment for sure for Jacob Cowing and and his teammates were really really happy for him. Uh David, keeping it in the wide receiver room with with one more um because you said Nick Bos is kind of a completely separate issue. For example, when Christian McCaffrey misses a bunch of time with air quotes tightness and then we find out later, ah this was actually just kind of the plan. Is the same thing going on with Mike Evans? Does he have a groin and a quad and an ankle or is this load management? >> I think it's load management. I'm I'm sure there's there's a little bit going on there, but it's football. That's the thing. It's it this is a sport, especially for guys who have a lot of mileage. And he had what 11 straight 1,000 yard season. So, he's played a lot of football. He's taken a lot of hits, but he's also shown the ability to stay available when it matters throughout his entire career. So, of course, uh he's going to be feeling stuff during during training camp, but you got to be smart. And you were there today, too. You saw Mike Evans joking around during team drills. He wasn't back in the ice tub or he wasn't back doing rehab out of sight. He was walking around just fine. I I still remember he was limping off the practice field last week in LA. And then uh a couple days later, I saw Mike Evans just fine at practice back in Santa Clara uh catching some big passes from Brock Perie. This is going to be, I predict, a continuous cycle over the course of this year. Mike Evans might be a little bit hobbled. People are going to freak out, but then when the money's down and he has to deliver, he's he's going to be out there. He's going to be playing. that's been the story of of uh Mike Evans career, especially the the later portions of it, and he's still been a productive player. So, as long as you can avoid the the big serious injuries, and I know last year was the year where those finally derailed his streak, but if you can go back to the 11 years before that, where you avoid those serious injuries, this guy's going to find a way to be out on the field when it matters. >> And that's the same story with McAffrey, avoiding those serious injuries. And David, I was looking at the last two healthy years, and when he's on the field, he gets a target or a touch nearly 50% of all plays. Would you anticipate the same level of workload? And if so, do they have to then get him off the field more often to protect him from himself? >> Well, I think you're already seeing a little bit of that, right? Because he had 380 something touches, I want to say, in 2023. That was that was a massive workload year. And then the Achilles tendinitis popped up in 2024 and derailed that season. So, uh, 2025 was a 413 touch here for McAffrey. So, it was even more of a workload than 2023. So, you could see the danger of the pattern here, right? Coming off of the heavy workload year. They didn't want this to turn into 2024 again. So, the whole 15-day absence from practice at training camp was all part of the plan to to back off on the workload. Now, will they also be able to back off on the workload within the actual game? Well, I think so. I think they've tried to set it up for that. I think that Kalon Black has looked really good for the 49ers. They used the third round pick on him. Jordan James is back at practice now. He he's also looked solid. I mean, the the upgrade button that they've pressed on the running back room over the past week with the return of those three guys, McCaffrey, Black, and Jordan James, has been really really palpable. You could you could just feel it out there on the field how much faster and stronger and more powerful they've gotten. But I think that the way that you preserve Christian McAffrey most is by actually having firepower at wide receiver. You know that that's what they really didn't have last year. And that's why McAffrey got so many touches because he was also the primary guy in the pass game. So Mike Evans, Dejon Stribbling, you know, the Jordan Watkins, you could talk about emergence of of of other players in that room. that that's what's going to allow you to space the field and and I think take some pressure off of Christian McAffrey on top of the obvious depth addition at running

title: Dan Patrick breaks down CTE study, how guardian caps can be embraced | Dan Patrick Show | NFL on NBC
text: I mentioned this study. So, 25% of all former NFL players who died during a 6-year period had CTE. That's the degenerative brain disease. That doesn't include nearly 3/4 of deceased players who weren't tested for the disease. Uh scientists say that 10 to 20% of coal miners who have worked 25 years or more have gotten black lung disease. Now, that's considered an epidemic. So, you can imagine at there's a former OSHA official, a scientist, said it's apocalyptically high the number that we have, noting that Russian roulette carries better odds. So, to him the risk of 1 in 100 would be an epidemic. You had 25% of all of these former players. We know it's there. We know it's not going away. And I wasn't surprised when I got the information. And maybe I'm numb to it because I've said before, it's next man up for us as fans. Like you love a player, but do you really stay in touch and find out how Earl Campbell's doing? And the answer is no. Jim McMahon. Go down the list. You know, when we had Eric Dickerson in studio, that was a couple of years ago, and he said, "I have to sleep in a chair. I have to sleep upright. I can't sleep in a bed." Now, once again, there's another running back, and there's another running back, and you know, all right, we move on with this. But when you see the totality of this, and yes, they sign up for this. Um these Guardian helmets, I know they look odd. And I think if there was a way to make them look a little bit more aesthetically pleasing, that players would be okay with this. We We know it's going to help protect your brain more than the regular NFL helmet, and they made great strides. But if they could do it where the protective covering looks better, then players might not feel like, you know, they have a bubble on their head. Keep in mind, Jacques Plante was the first goalie to wear a mask. Now, can you imagine what the reaction must have been? Like, "What is wrong with him?" "Oh, he's soft. He's wearing a mask." You know, when you had you know, these players wearing shields in hockey. And these are the toughest guys. Baseball batting helmets. You imagine? Wait. He's got a batting helmet on? Remember you know, the the flap, you know, protecting you know, the left or right side of your face. And now we just accept it. It's okay. With a batting helmet. Barry Bonds going up there looking like a gladiator with all the padding on his arm. Like we just kind of accept it. And I'm wondering, can we get to the point where NFL players, college players, and I don't know the cost of that for college players, but college is a bigger problem than the NFL, folks. Because they don't get the medical treatment. Nobody is following up with them when they graduate, and only 2% of college football players play in the NFL. That's the epidemic. That's That's the silent epidemic that no one is talking about. The college players who are doing whatever it takes to get to the NFL. And then when you don't, you just kind of fall into society. But you're in it with probably CTE. But I think if they got the Guardian helmets to look better. Like it looks odd and I get it. But like I said, a hockey mask. You imagine the other goalies going like how soft is he? Or somebody's wearing a batting helmet. Oh man, Bonds wearing all that armor. Now we we we accept it. We're okay. We We pad the walls in NASCAR. Remember that was a big deal? Oh, come on. You know, that's that's on NASCAR? We We didn't have outfield walls in baseball with padding. You'd run into brick at Wrigley Field. Like who would have thought that would be a good idea? Now we pad the walls. >> [laughter] >> It seems crazy at the time where you go, yeah, I don't know why we didn't pad those. But I think it's the aesthetics that may bother people bother athletes of what you wear. But I think if we can get past that, boy, it'd be great if you're able to reduce that number. >> Yeah, Paul. >> We went back and looked at adding helmets in baseball and actually started in the early 1900s, but they had these leather caps like football had and the players were sweating and couldn't deal with it. So they went away. And then they decided a nice wool cap will protect your head for the next 40 years. And then in the 50s, it actually started with Little League baseball. They mandated protective headgear for all games. And then 1956, the National League did it. A couple years later, the American League did it, but it took a while and they actually grandfathered players in kind of like hockey. If you started before 1956, you didn't have to wear a helmet. It was your choice. Hockey did this as well. It didn't really become official official till 1971 and everyone had to wear >> And then When look at NFL helmets. They're They're football helmets. Like they were leather When my father played, he had a leather helmet on, no face mask, and he broke his nose nine times. So, it's your face is open there. And then all of a sudden they had like this plastic shield that you would wear. I mean, the players were dying. They were going to outlaw football. Back in the, you know, 1912, Roosevelt, I think, was outlawing football because it was so violent. And then all of a sudden you got a helmet. And then you got a chin strap. And then you got a mouthpiece. And guys with Joe Theismann had the single bar. I'm thinking, that ain't protecting anything, Joe. Yeah, Dylan. >> Yeah, I think it's easy to like overreact to maybe the advancements in the safety of sports in the moment, but then you look back like in, you know, probably X amount of years, the people look at the Guardian cap and be like, that's all they were wearing? Like even Well, who was Was it Gerry Cheevers who would draw these the stitches on So, like, they wore this mask and got made fun of. You were still getting hit in the face with a hockey puck. Like, it was still pressed against your face. So, it's like, in the moment it looks weird. You evolve. >> And I [snorts] hope that 30 years from now people will look back and go, "Oh, oh, so that's when they started using the Guardian helmets." And maybe some radio show, if they have radio shows in 30 years from now, will talk about our show and say, "You know, I remember when I was growing up and Dan Patrick was calling for the Guardian helmet." Got to make him look a little bit better. I think players will be okay because it does look like you got a big fishbowl on your on your shoulders there. Even shoulder pads. Uh guys don't even wear thigh pads. They don't wear knee pads. Like you'll watch somebody come out and they'll be Oh my god. You basically just have a pair of pants on. Like you have Capri pants on you're out there playing football. So that was that that came out yesterday. I think it was like British Medical Journal that released the information here, but I'm not I'm not surprised. But it is an epidemic. And I have two friends who know they have CTE, former players. They know it. They don't acknowledge it. They said there's nothing I can do. You want to make sure you take care of your family. They want to make sure and they are in their 50s. They want to make sure they're not a burden to their families. That's their number one thing that they're thinking of when it comes to their health. You don't want to be an invalid. You don't want to have 24/7 care. But they know that's probably on the way. You don't know when, but you know it's on the way. And it's hard to be a Like you want to bring it up and like I see them slipping. I I see them when they talk to me and they'll kind of zone out a little bit or they'll stop. Uh the lights bother them. Bright lights really bother them. And they don't know how many concussions cuz they said, you know, we got our bell rung. You know, just a whole different mentality. So whenever I see Tua Tagovailoa, like I hope he's okay. But he's signing up to continue to play this. He's getting well compensated. I just don't know. I mean there's inherent risk, you know it. Um but it's one of those you really don't know until somebody you know has it. Or somebody you know dies. And then they discover this. That's when it starts to hit home. These guys are 24 years old, 25, 26. They're not afraid. Or they compartmentalize that. So these numbers I don't want to be numb to them, but I am. I just I'm not surprised. Yes, Mark. >> You got to play devil's advocate a bit. When you see these guys that they sign up for it, but they love the game. They love football. And so a lot of times you the game you love and you're getting compensated for it, it's hard to say I'm going to stop doing it. >> Yeah. I I I wouldn't I wouldn't stop. And I talked to my wife about my son playing football. And I said, it's up and I grew up in a football family. But I said it, you know, does he want to play? And he's big enough to have played, but he wanted to play other sports. And I said that that's I'm I was relieved. I did not want him playing football. But if he wanted to play, I was going to be right there for him. I get it. If I was good enough or I was playing now and I'm making good kind of money, taking care of my family, yeah. Cuz we all say the same thing. Won't happen to me. And you can't play a different way. I can't That's I I couldn't have Ronnie Lott played differently. I couldn't have Junior Seau played differently. Troy Polamalu, Ray Lewis, Rodney Harrison, this is how they played. So when you say, "Oh, you know, maybe don't use your head or don't be vi- whatever." You you can't think like that. You react when you're on a football field. You react as an athlete. You can't go like oh wait a minute, what am I supposed to do? You don't have time to think. It's not golf. You don't have time to think. You play the way you've played. >> Yeah, but I'm >> And the irony is if you're not good, you'll stop. The game will stop you. Like you get the end of your high school like nobody wants you to play college, it's over. So you cut down those hits. But now the money in pro football is getting bigger and bigger. So if you have a good first few years, yeah, I'll I'll sign up for five more years. It's five more years of hits but you're getting 25 million a year. There's not an incentive for you to stop. >> The better you are, the more likely it is you'll have CTE.

And it was right after the Scobel trade, etc., etc. Before we get into that, can I weigh in on this whole Brown LSU thing? >> Yes. >> That That's just a blip on the radar, and it's a symptomatic of something larger. And it's this. This isn't just corrupt or chaotic, it's both of those things. It's now at a point where it's perverse. But, it doesn't What happens with the Browns and LSU is just a blip on the radar screen, or it's a relatively insignificant. Take a step back. When NIL was first suggested, what all of us understood it to mean was this. If a kid is at a university, and he happens to have a musical talent, and if the orchestra in that town wants him or her to play in the orchestra, then why shouldn't they be able to be paid, even if they're a scholarship athlete? Why shouldn't a guy in College Station be able to make a hundred grand from the local car dealer if he's a star quarterback? That's what it meant. Not the university directly paying them to attend. Now, there could have been other reforms. There could have been a stipend across the board where everybody who's on scholarship gets the same, whether they're a bench player or or a star. They could have done that. And provisions that Dale Brown, for example, at LSU, ironically, talked about years and years ago. Like, I can't reach into my own pocket and pay a kid that I recruited and brought here, give him enough money to fly home because his grandmother died, to fly home for the funeral. All those reforms should have been in place. But, the idea that you'll directly pay players to attend a university undermines the exact purpose of what a university is. And all of the university presidents who sit mum because they realize how important the basketball and football programs are to the university, all of them who don't speak up are very much like 99% of the Republicans in Congress and in the Senate who won't speak up even though they know what's happening right in front of them is perverse. >> Well, I mean, it all started, Bob, July 1st, 2021.
